She decided to take in four boys with intellectual disabilities as day scholars in the schools. She took in a girl, a fresh graduate, and trained and taught her the finer points of teaching children with intellectual difficulties. She also hired two care-givers to start with.

Then began Manjulaa Kalyaan’s journey of shifting houses as the strength of both students as well as resident girls increased. In a way, she had already initiated the concept of Group Home long before it was recognized under the Inclusion Act in 2007.

Cut to 2026, Swayamkrushi which Manjulaa Kalyaan had dared to dream in 1991, is now a full-blown Not-for-Profit Organisation, and home to about 75 persons, mostly young adult girls with intellectual disabilities and a school with a total strength of about 150. The organization, now located in its own five-acre campus in Jawahar Nagar, also conducts a two-year B.Ed in Special Education (Intellectual Disabilities) and it boasts of a staff strength of about 70.

The organization has all the required specialized areas and tools including Group Homes, integration with the real world, speech therapy, art therapy, music therapy, regular classes, NIOS and vocational training and support through paper bag making, printing and tailoring units. And a full fledged kitchen dining hall to cater to the needs of the residents.

title: A Home of Care, Growth and Hope
excerpt: Any person visiting Swayakrushi for the first time would probably be surprised at the seemingly unguarded huge open gate that beckons you in, and as you make your way in, you are more likely to be greeted by a herd of cows on one side and b...
paragraphs: (Long form stories)

Any person visiting Swayakrushi for the first time would probably be surprised at the seemingly unguarded huge open gate that beckons you in, and as you make your way in, you are more likely to be greeted by a herd of cows on one side and birds chirping from the branches of several fruit-bearing trees and flowering plants on the other. Enter the building and you will be met by Akhila Hemmali and Tanuj Goyal, both persons with intellectual disabilities, at the front desk. Akhila with a smile would ask you to log in your details in a register. And if you enter the office right behind the front desk and ask Phanindra for some help or direction, he may not be ‘loud and clear’ but would nevertheless guide you willingly. Phani has hearing impairment but he is an important cog in the administrative wheel.

These elements that one encounters essentially convey the Mission Statement of the 35-year-old organization at its very basic – Empowerment, unfettered openness and the importance of nature for the development of special persons, mostly adult girls, living in the premises.

Founded in 1991 by Manjulaa Kalyaan, the award-winning NGO has been a pioneer in rehabilitating and integrating adults with intellectual disabilities, and more importantly, spearheading the Group Homes concept which it initiated 16 years before it was officially recognised through the Inclusion Act in 2007. The organisation has also been striving hard to increase the reach of the movement for inclusion across Telangana and beyond.

In a nutshell, Swayamkrushi’s Mission is to house and train Persons with Intellectual Disabilities, facilitate their employment and subsequently independent living within the community. Our vision is to build a society in which the less fortunate persons get an opportunity to live with dignity and pride and as productive members of the society. And the Group Homes concept is a crucial and critical part in our approach where each home houses eight trainees with different levels of intellectual disabilities. They are managed by a resident staff member and the efforts are aimed at residential support, therapy, vocational training, and community integration.
Working with a set of core values

Over time, Swayamkrushi has established a set of core values that give direction to the organisation and this has become an inherent and integral part of the staff psyche. Firstly, the organisation has always believed that compassion precedes everything that it does, which essentially means that every decision, programme, and interaction is guided by deep compassion and genuine care for the individuals it serves. We have embraced the holistic growth approach under which we nurture the person as a whole - intellectual, emotional, social, and vocational because growth has to be multidimensional.

The approach would not serve the purpose in its entirety if dignity and respect of individuals is not ensured. To that end, every person in Swayamkrushi is treated with the highest dignity and his or her personhood acknowledged and celebrated at every step. Most importantly and as part of our efforts for effective inclusion, we also strive to build bridges between our community and the broader society, fostering genuine inclusion at every level. And in these fast-changing times, we also are continuously striving to improve our methods, programmes and facilities to deliver the best possible outcomes.

Lastly, we are very particular about accountability of all actions, since the ‘open book’ policy is very close to the heart of the founder-director Manjulaa Kalyaan. The organisation maintains absolute transparency with its stakeholders, families, and donors through regular updates and publication of annual reports and regular updates.
The heart and soul of Swayamkrushi

Needless to say, the heart and soul of Swayamkrushi is Manjulaa Kalyaan who has dedicated over three decades to empowering not only persons with intellectual disabilities but also women. A visionary educator who is considered a doyenne in this field, Manjulaa Kalyaan has been the recipient of several awards and recognition at the highest level nationally including personal acknowledgement by former President late Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam. Her inventiveness and tireless compassion have shaped every aspect of Swayamkrushi's approach, programmes and lasting impact. The organisation is fortunate to have in its Managing Committee people with complete dedication to the cause. In the words of Manjulaa Kalyaan: "Swayamkrushi is run by a committee of passionate and experienced members. We are a team that believes in the core values, which is why we want to protect and harness the skill we are entrusted with by training these individuals."

In essence, Swayamkrushi empowers Persons with Intellectual Disabilities with personalized educational programs, vocational skill development training, and independent living skills with a comprehensive range of programs designed to support individuals across different stages of development with dignity.

Little wonder that the organisation has grown to such levels given the fact that Manjulaa Kalyaan’s strongpoint has been her conviction about the work she does and the passion she carries in her heart. “I do what nobody else does,” declares the octogenarian founder-director of Swayamkrushi.
Bullet Points
Empowerment of persons with intellectual disabilities, women main objectives of Swayamkrushi
Swayamkrushi is a pioneer in Group Homes, initiating the concept 16 years before its recognition under Inclusive Act in 2007
Core values - Compassion, holistic growth, dignity of individual, accountability

Contact us by phone or email to arrange an initial visit and assessment. Our team will guide you through the admission process and available programmes.
What age groups do you serve?
We serve children from school age through adulthood. Our programmes are tailored to the individual's developmental stage, not strictly by age.
Are there residential facilities?
Yes, we offer 24/7 residential care with full supervision, meals, healthcare support, and participation in all programmes.
Can I volunteer at Swayamkrushi?
Absolutely. We welcome volunteers with skills in education, therapy, arts, administration, and more. Fill the contact form and select "Volunteer" to get started.

A minimum of 80 per cent of every donation goes directly to programmes and care. Full details are published in our Annual Reports.

Yes, the B.Ed Special Education programme is affiliated with Osmania University and certified by the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI).

title: Group Homes — A Pioneering Initiative Ahead of Its Time
excerpt: Group Home – a pioneering initiative ahead of time
paragraphs: (Long form stories)
Group Home – a pioneering initiative ahead of time

Swayamkrushi is well-known all over the country for the work it has been doing in extending care to persons with intellectual disabilities. But the singular initiative that brought the Institute fame and accolades was the introduction of Group Homes, a concept that was thought of and conceived by founder-director Manjulaa Kalyaan way back in 1991, a full 16 years ahead of the concept’s ratification by the Government of India through the Inclusion Act in 2007.

The Group Homes concept, not experimented anywhere in the country till the totally unique idea was implemented by Swayamkrushi in Hyderabad, helped adult girls with intellectual disabilities to live, work and learn in natural domestic environment. For this challenging task, the institute rented houses in residential colonies that would help train the young girls to integrate with the society.

Each of these Group Homes comprise eight women (all above the age of 18) with different levels of intellectual disabilities, living together akin to extended Indian families. Each single group comprises three women in the mild range, four in moderate range and one from the severe range. The first seven are trained to take care of the house as also the woman with severe challenges.

“And I am proud to say that Swayamkrushi has five such homes now, all located in residential colonies that are in close proximity to the Institute to facilitate their participation in the institute’s training sessions and classes,” says Manjulaa Kalyaan with a broad smile, revealing the pride she takes in having introduced the initiative in India much ahead of its time.

This programme not only provides a healthy opportunity to these women for independent living and community integration but also simultaneously creates awareness in the surrounding community facilitating the acceptance of people with intellectual disabilities.
Recipe for Independent Living

Swayamkrushi has worked out its own three-pronged curriculum for Independent Living (IL) that comprises training for Home Living Skills, development of Community Living Skills and preparation for the World of Work. The curriculum is tailored to provide family life for young people with intellectual disabilities including the warmth, routine, and belonging that comes from living together as a household under caring supervision.
Under the Home Living Skills, the young adults are trained in personal care, home maintenance, cooking, clothing care and spending leisure time.
The Community Living Skills involves training in mobility through daily commutes and using public transport, managing stores and services, visiting restaurants and recreational activities.

When it comes to the critical World of Work part, they go through the process of job surveys, finding placements and on-the-job training. The process also involves maintenance support of the Institute during the critical initial stages, gradual withdrawal and finally follow-up of their development and progress.
The Group Homes objectives

The entire process, essentially the objectives of the Group Homes project, is to initiate persons with intellectual disabilities to the daily routine of living at home and within a community, provide opportunities to face normal developmental experiences and create a structured environment rich in sensory stimulation. The process also helps in easing them into the idea of living in one place, working in another and enjoying their leisure time in a variety of places. It also fosters independent use of money through realistic financial management training.
…And the rewards

The reward for introducing the Group Homes concept comes unexpectedly in various forms as Manjulaa Kalyaan explains. “Take for instance the experience of the girls in one of the homes when they realized that the gas cylinder was empty one evening. They approached a neighbour, explained their situation and even convinced them into using their kitchen to make rotis. In another case, two girls came up with a precise list of their requirements. This for me is the ultimate reward, something that gave me utmost satisfaction since the girls were thinking independently. That for me is the ultimate achievement,” she goes on to add.

Manjulaa Kalyaan’s efforts brought her several awards including the National Award for Welfare of People with Disabilities by former President late Dr. A.P.J. Abdul Kalam, for her pioneering work, particularly in promoting the Group Homes concept.
Bullet Points
Group Homes help adult girls with ID to live, work and learn in natural domestic environment
Each group comprises three women in mild range, four in moderate range and one from severe range
IL curriculum comprises training for home living skills, development of community living skills and preparation for world of work

title: Swayamkrushi — The B.Ed Hotspot

Swayamkrushi is a much sought after institute when it comes to pursuing a degree in special education focusing on persons with intellectual disabilities. The B.Ed Special Education programme at Swayamkrushi, which began in 2008, is a two-year, full-time degree course affiliated with Osmania University. The institute has been churning out dozens of graduates year after year who are job-ready for placement in schools, NGOs, rehabilitation centres and government institutions.

Swayamkrushi, which has sent out about 1,000 highly competent and successful rehabilitation professionals so far, has an annual student intake capacity of 30. The factors that make the institute a hot spot for B.Ed in Special Education include a highly professional and totally dedicated faculty, many of whom have worked in some of the country’s leading institutes in the field, insistence on mandatory attendance of at least 80 per cent, activity- and evidence-based learning and more importantly, practical-based training. Another major factor is the cost of the course which is probably the lowest in the field.

This formula of combining theoretical learning with extensive field practice ensures that the programme equips students with the competencies to design and deliver inclusive, child-centred education for students with intellectual disabilities.

In the first year of the B.Ed course for Special Education, the emphasis is on foundation, theory and practicals. In the process, the students are exposed to the philosophy and sociology of education that includes human growth and development, introduction to disabilities, education of students with disabilities, intervention and teaching strategies, equitable and inclusive education and curriculum development, adaptation and evaluation (ID) in the theory side spread over two semesters. Besides, the students are put through the grind of practicals that cover disability and inclusion, disability specialisation, lesson planning, development of TLM and teaching, subject teaching in regular schools and supportive skill training.

In the second year, the students are taught life skills across life span, supportive skills for education of children with disabilities, digital technologies in education, psycho-social and family issues (ID), skill-based optional course, basic research and basic statistics, employability skills and Indian Knowledge Systems in the two semesters.

The continuing and extensive practicals in the second year cover lesson planning and execution at different levels for all subjects, teaching in regular schools and more importantly, internship in disability specialisation, internship at inclusive school as also in other disability special schools.

By the time the students complete the B.Ed course, they are ready to teach and support students with intellectual disabilities in schools, join impactful NGOs involved in rehabilitation, education and community inclusion, work alongside therapists in residential and day-care facilities providing integrated support. They are also qualified with RCI recognised credentials for government teachers’ posts besides taking on disability welfare roles. Based on their aptitude, the graduates from Swayamkrushi can also provide home-based support by extending structured, professional support to families caring for persons with intellectual disabilities.

Explaining the advantage that Swayamkrushi graduates enjoy, the college Principal M Sarada says: “The interview process is that much easier for our graduates since the institute is known for its focus on both academics and practicals, and its insistence on mandatory attendance. They are already well-trained in the field and well-versed with the subject and are job-ready when they leave the institute.”

Adds PVB Sudhakar, Assistant Professor in Special Education and Head of the Department at Swayamkrushi. “In fact, such is the popularity of Swayamkrushi’s B.Ed degree that many describe it as a visa to go abroad, particularly the US. Every year, at least 75 per cent of the students find placements abroad and the remaining land jobs locally even before completing the course.”

The Institute, Sarada goes on to point out, also conducts six programmes every year on “Continuing Rehabilitation Education (CRE) which is meant for professionals to upgrade their skills and knowledge. “It is also important to note that we have a barrier-free environment and the facilities for students include ramp, lift, washrooms, drinking water and spacious classrooms, a well-stacked library, a digital lab, resource room and hostel facilities,” says the Principal.

The Institute, as part of its expansion plans, will soon be introducing a two-year Master’s Degree in Special Education (Intellectual disability), B.Ed (Learning Disability), Diploma in Special Education (Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities) for students who have completed Intermediate, and a two-year Diploma in Vocational Rehabilitation (ID), again for students who have completed Intermediate.

Also in the pipeline is the construction of a new building block that would house all the academic activities of Swayamkrushi, moving a step closer to the organisation’s founder-director Manjulaa Kalyaan’s dream. “My ultimate dream is to convert the Institute into a Deemed University, and we are moving in that direction gradually,” says Manjulaa Kalyaan, who has obviously set her sights firmly on a much higher orbit.
Bullet points
1,000 highly competent and successful rehabilitation professionals passed out so far from Swayamkrushi
80 per cent of students from Swayamkrushi find placements abroad every year, rest assured of local jobs before completing course
Equal focus on practical and theory, 80 per cent attendance mandatory
activity- and evidence-based learning, practical-based training, low cost of course hallmarks of Swayamkrushi B.Ed

In the pipeline are a two-year Master’s Degree in Special Education (ID), B.Ed (Learning Disability), Diploma in Special Education (Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities), two-year Diploma in Vocational Rehabilitation (ID)

paragraphs: Right Shoulder

The Covid years, dreaded as they were, also had its positives, opening up clogged minds of several people trapped in their homes, as they looked for avenues to augment their shrinking income. Many came up with brilliant business ideas that soon took root as ‘startups,’ a term that had just begun making a big buzz in India for new businesses in the Internet and e-commerce era. But not all were looking for means to convert the depressing situation into monetary opportunities, and a case in point is that of Manjulaa Kalyaan, the founder-director of Swayamkrushi.

In fact, what caught Manjulaa’s attention and sowed the seeds of opportunity for humanitarian service in her mind was a small newspaper report about a boy with intellectual disabilities, unaware that his single mother had died of Covid and continued staying in the house for a couple of days before the deathly stench alerted neighbours. A disturbed Manjulaa, who has been taking care of persons with intellectual disabilities and interacting with their families for well over three decades, immediately saw the potential and the need to help such families. She came up with ‘Parent Homes,’ a unique one-bedroom in-campus dwelling initiative under which such helpless families can also be brought under the umbrella and care of Swayamkrushi.

The house-on-lease concept virtually signalled the shifting of the stress and trauma that parents of children with intellectual disabilities undergo, to Swayamkrushi since these children attend classes and other activities in the school during the day and return to their parents late in the evening. “The unique feature of this facility is that the parents can continue to stay in the unit for their lifetime if the child passes away, and in the event of the parents passing away, we take care of the child for life,” points out Manjulaa Kalyaan.

Says A Purushottama Rao, father of 26-year-old A Hrishikesa who was afflicted with cerebral palsy at birth: “This parent housing is nothing but a blessing for parents like us. Both me and my wife Chandrika are retired persons and we were clueless and helpless as to what the future holds for our family. We grabbed this opportunity when Manjulaa Madam offered it to us and have been living on the campus since October of 2024. I have no words to describe the humanitarian service that Manjulaa Madam has been rendering for families like ours. Her dedication and commitment to the cause is unparalleled.”

A retired Assistant General Manager of HMT, Purushottama Rao and Chandrika, a retired Union Bank of India employee, place Manjulaa Kalyaan in the same pedestal as that of God. “For us, she is God. She and the organization have virtually taken over our problems and stress since we shifted here. Hrishikesa is very happy in the school. We make sure that he only eats what is served by the organization keeping in mind his future needs. Our idea is that he should get used to the people, the environment and the food here so that he won’t have any issues later in future when we are not there,” says the 69-year-old native of Krishna district in Andhra Pradesh, who can’t stop talking about the ‘kindness and dedication’ of Manjulaa Kalyaan.

Candidly speaking about the distress and helplessness that they endured before Hrishikesa joined Swayamkrushi in 2022 and their shifting to the campus subsequently, Purushottama Rao points out that they explored all options available in the city, the various special schools and other facilities, but were not happy with any of them. “It was during our constant search for a suitable special school for Hrishikesa that we came across Swayamkrushi. Once he was admitted here, everything began to fall into place, and our life took a different turn, more so after we opted for the parent housing scheme. In fact, believe it or not, both I and my wife were having issues with our health earlier, but after shifting to Swayamkrushi, our health has improved and that is because we are very comfortable both mentally and physically. We are very lucky and feel proud to declare that we are now part of the Swayamkrushi family,” says a beaming Purushottama Rao.

Summing up the family’s current situation that finds echo with other parents in similar position, the retired HMT employee says: “A day will come when Hrishikesa may be alone, but we are not worried since he will have the Swayamkrushi family behind him then.”

title: The Mysterious Appearance of Shirdi Sai Baba
excerpt: The mysterious ‘appearance’ of Shirdi Sai Baba
paragraphs: (Fun Facts)
The mysterious ‘appearance’ of Shirdi Sai Baba

On a warm summer afternoon in 2015, a courier presented himself at the Swayamkrushi office, then located on the first floor of a building in Trimulgherry, and announced that he was there to deliver a ‘parcel.’ The organisation’s founder-director Manjulaa Kalyaan casually remarked “send it up.” “It’s big and heavy,” the courier delivery person said, to which she replied: “Take the lift and bring it up.” He, however, insisted that she come down. Left with no choice, Manjulaa Kalyaan went down and lo and behold was her ‘parcel,’ a huge wooden crate atop a truck parked in front of her office.

Completely stumped by the size of the ‘parcel,’ Manjulaa Kalyaan asked the courier to deliver the crate at the new campus site in Chennapur near Jawahar Nagar, where a crane had to be brought in to bring it down from the truck. The crate was placed in the under-construction building in the five-acre campus.

Manjulaa Kalyaan and her colleagues including then B.Ed principal late Durga Shankar were completely clueless about what was inside the crate. All that they knew was that the parcel had originated in Nashik in neighbouring Maharashtra and had the Swayamkrushi address for delivery. They were unwilling to unravel the mystery of the parcel for some time at least for fear of it being a case of wrong delivery or wrong address. Curiosity, however, got the better of Durga who one day peered through a gap in the wooden crate and jumped back at being met by the piercing gaze from a pair of eyes in an idol.

After holding on to the ‘parcel’ for three months, Manjulaa Kalyaan decided to have the crate dismantled and there it was, a resplendent marble replica of Shirdi Sai Baba, standing all of six-and-half feet!

“After much confabulation over where the majestic idol should be placed, it was decided, as per Vaastu, to have it consecrated in a prayer hall to be built right beside the gate. The consecration was done strictly as per “Shaastra,’ a purohut was hired to conduct daily aarti and special puja is conducted on the occasion of Guru Purnima, when all the children from the institute gather at the prayer hall,” recalls a misty-eyed Manjulaa Kalyaan.
That was how the mysterious ‘visitor’ from Nashik came to reside permanently in Swayamkrushi.

paragraphs: (fun facts)

The going wasn’t easy for Manjulaa Kalyaan when she first set up Swayamkrushi to make her dream of caring for girls with intellectual disabilities a reality. Equipped as she was with tons of experience in the field having worked with various organisations in the same line besides a masters in special education, Manjula realised that she would have to think of ingenuous ways to raise resources to run the organisation. That was when she hit upon the brilliant idea of launching the “DOS” club to tap the women in her neighbourhood for resources. DOS, in case you are scratching your head over what it meant, was just ‘Dal, Oil, Sugar’ - plain and simple.

Manjula asked the womenfolk in her neighbourhood to buy an extra kg of these three commodities or any other kitchen ingredient for that matter when they go shopping for their monthly groceries. The idea was a runaway success!

In another novel initiative, she visited some schools carrying a closed box with an opening on top. She attended the school assemblies, explained to the children the plight of their less fortunate brethren in Swayamkrushi, and asked them to bring something that they used on a daily basis and drop it in the box. It could be a toothbrush, a comb, a cake of soap or a shampoo sachet. And soon enough, the boxes she placed in the school premises were full with such simple stuff which she used for ‘her children’ in the organisation.
How’s that for thinking out of the box?

title: Visa to Go Abroad
excerpt: Did you know that obtaining a degree in special education from Swayamkrushi virtually served as a visa to go abroad, particularly the US?
paragraphs: (Fun Facts)
Did you know that obtaining a degree in special education from Swayamkrushi virtually served as a visa to go abroad, particularly the US?

Well, every year, about 75 per cent to 80 per cent of the students graduating from the Institute find placements abroad. This should not come as a surprise as the Institute has been occupying the numero uno position in Osmania University year after year, grabbing the gold medal in special education for intellectual disabilities almost every year since the B.Ed course was introduced in 2007.

“On one of my visits to the US, I found 36 special educators who had graduated from Swayamkrushi working in Atlanta alone. Similarly, you will come across dozens of special educators from Swayamkrushi working in South Carolina and Mississippi,” points out the Institute’s founder-director Manjulaa Kalyaan.

So, what makes graduates from Swayamkrushi stand out in the crowd? “The interview process is that much easier for our graduates since the institute is known for its focus on both academics and practicals, and its insistence on mandatory attendance. They are already well-trained in the field and well-versed with the subject and are job-ready when they leave the institute,” says Dr PVB Sudhakar, Assistant Professor in Special Education and Head of the Department at Swayamkrushi.

While the Institute is not averse to the graduates seeking greener pastures abroad, Manjulaa Kalyaan realized that they were losing out on precious local talent. To check the trend to some extent, the Institute recently introduced a three-year bond for candidates seeking admission for B.Ed course under which they would have to work with Swayamkrushi during the bond period.
Thus began a three-year waiting period for the aspirants, but still worth it!

title: 15 Years for One Word, and Then the Exhilaration!
filename: 15 years for one word, and then the exhilaration!.docx
excerpt: When 15-year-old Sai uttered the word ‘Amma” one day, tears of joy rolled down the cheeks of D Dora Babu, the speech therapist at Swayamkrushi. This was the reward he was waiting for after weeks of effort put in to help Sai, who besides hav...
paragraphs: To go in Shoulder

When 15-year-old Sai uttered the word ‘Amma” one day, tears of joy rolled down the cheeks of D Dora Babu, the speech therapist at Swayamkrushi. This was the reward he was waiting for after weeks of effort put in to help Sai, who besides having hearing impairment also suffers from intellectual disabilities. This was the first word to tumble out of Sai’s mouth in 15 years and Babu’s exhilaration was justifiably palpable.

The speech therapy unit in Swayamkrushi at present has 10 students, all of them with intellectual disabilities and hearing impairment. Babu uses flash cards, mirror, picture cards, toys and story books, among other things, as tools to help the children say a few words if not sentences. “The mirror in my class room is an important tool as it facilitates oral motor exercise. It helps the students focus on lip movement and imitate, thereby pronouncing some words,” says Babu, who has done D.Ed Special (Hearing Impairment) in Nandyal, Andhra Pradesh.

Babu also has a fascinating story to narrate why he chose this line of work. “I come from Chennur near Nandyal and in our neighbourhood, I came across some children with hearing impairment. They were attending regular government schools but didn’t learn anything since the schools did not have special educators who could have helped them. It was then I decided to do something for such children and came across this course in Nandyal,” says the 30-year-old speech therapist whose sister is also a teacher at Swayamkrushi.

Babu, who initially worked as a teacher in schools for the hearing impaired in AP, then came to know that there were children with both hearing impairment and intellectual disabilities, and this new desire to do something for such children brought him to Swayamkrushi in 2023.

Babu, who joined as assistant speech therapist at Swayamkrushi, is keen on doing a regular course that would help in handling such special children. “I have been managing so far with the knowledge I gained while doing the diploma since hearing impairment was also a subject,” says the determined therapist.

Explaining further the methodology adopted for his students, Babu says he uses different materials and tools for different students like blowing out a candle or blowing through a straw to help them imitate certain sounds based on phonetics. “It is mostly through lip movement and physical vibrations in the vocal cords that we teach the children some words. Ideally, speech therapy should be initiated before the age of six since the vocal cords are flexible at this age. It becomes difficult as the child grows. And this therapy is essentially individual-based meaning I can take only one student at a time,” points out Babu.

What gives him most satisfaction in this job? “My effort is to defeat the silence in the lives of these children. The moment they make a sound is the moment I cherish. For example, it took me weeks of effort on a daily basis to make Sai say the word ‘Amma,’ says Babu.

The efforts of the speech therapist in the past three years have paid off. Today, his students speak a few words. Tanushree, a 10-year-old girl, knows about 70 words while 12-year-old Ashi knows about 90 words. “That for me is the biggest reward,” says Babu, who enjoys his time with the students and vice-versa.

title: Hard Work Never Goes Unrewarded!
excerpt: (To go in ‘Way to Go’ - Right Shoulder)
paragraphs: (To go in ‘Way to Go’ - Right Shoulder)

When G Aruna joined Swayamkrushi as a gardener in 2020, little would she have known then that her decision would prove to be a game-changer in her life. Raised by a single mother struggling to keep afloat in Siddipet, Aruna was put through the grind of poverty but she kept her interest in education alive, even though by her own admission, she was petrified of English and Math. Her story reads like a script meant for people who are going through the roller-coaster ride of life and are on the precipice from where everything around seems hopeless.

Aruna lost her father when she was just a four-year-old kid and her sister just a baby, leaving her mother with the inheritance of poverty. She was witness to the struggle, but that only made her even more determined to educate herself. Despite the cruel financial background, Aruna, through sheer determination, managed to go through school, and then a B.A. degree too, from Jangaon. Even as a youngster, Aruna juggled between books and farm implements as she helped her mother in the farm to keep the wolves away from the door.

Along the way, as she grew up, Aruna dabbled in various small jobs after acquiring some training in spoken English and marketing from the District Rural Development Agency (DRDA), even as she pursued her degree course. “I took up a marketing job with Eureka Forbes but had to give it up a year later since I had to take care of my mother who had fallen ill,” says the 34-year-old woman, fighting back her tears.

Around this time, Aruna landed a seat in MBA at the Osmania University Post Graduate college in Siddipet. That was another feather in her cap. “I also got married while I was studying for MBA, gave birth to the first of my three children, but still managed to get 75 per cent in the examination. But then, I had to stay at home to take care of the children till they reached an age where I could return to work, and that took nine years,” recollects Aruna.

It was in 2020 that an acquaintance and neighbour, Sarada, suggested that she approach Swayamkrushi for a job. Sarada works as a cook in the organization. “I didn’t reveal my educational qualifications for fear of being rejected. Given my farming background, I landed a job as a gardener. After working for some time, Manjula Madam came to know that I was an MBA graduate and suggested that I do B.Ed in special education that would help me get a teacher’s job in the organization,” she points out with misty eyes.

She was admitted for the B.Ed course in 2022 and completed it in 2024, and was soon appointed as teacher in the Swayamkrushi school for persons with intellectual disabilities. “Manjula Madam not only took care of the course cost for two years but also continued to pay me salary during the entire period. The sensitive person that she is, Manjula Madam also shifted me to work in the stores as an assistant to avoid any kind of embarrassment as a student,” recalls Aruna, and goes on to add that life has been kind to her of late.

“I have achieved my goal of doing something in life. All this was possible only because of Manjula Madam and I will ever remain grateful to her for that. I am also enjoying my job as a special educator, which calls for a lot of patience and understanding. The children in my class are very attached to me just as I am fond of them,” says Aruna.
Isn’t Aruna’s story truly inspiring that at once reaffirms our belief in the saying that hard work never goes unrewarded?

title: Luck, Hard Work and Guardian Angel Spell Success
filename: Luck, hard work and guardian angel spell success.docx
excerpt: (Long form under ‘Way to Go’ – Right Shoulder)
paragraphs: (Long form under ‘Way to Go’ – Right Shoulder)

Luck, as the adage goes, favours the brave and the hard-working. For J Srilata, it was not merely luck that was on her side but also Manjulaa Kalyaan, the founder-director of Swayamkrushi, and time, that precious and unseen element capable of making or marring a person.

Hailing from an impoverished farmers’ family in Siddipet district, Srilata, one of five siblings, was the only one in the family who was determined to make a mark in life. Struggle was a constant companion for the 33-year-old woman but so were ambition and determination, and this made for a heady concoction of circumstances and emotions that could only end in success. Srilatha is now on the threshold of becoming a special educator at the Swayamkrushi school for persons with intellectual disabilities, a quantum jump from the post of ayah that she currently holds in the school.

Srilata, who has the uncanny knack of spotting an opportunity when it presents itself in the most unforeseeable circumstances, saw one when she was asked to help out Manjulaa Kalyaan at home after a surgery in 2022. Nobody in the organization was aware that she was a degree dropout because of financial constraints and that she had a burning desire, albeit suppressed, to make something of her life.

Initially very hesitant and even scared, Srilata slowly opened up to the octogenarian founder of the organization about her life, circumstances and dreams. Ever willing to take on the role of guardian angel, Manjulaa Kalyaan took to the young woman. “You complete your degree with a minimum of 50 per cent and I will ensure that you get admitted in the B.Ed (Special Education for ID), and I will also protect your salary as ayah while you study. Once you complete B.Ed, you will be absorbed in the school as special educator,” Manjulaa Kalyaan told the mother of two.

An elated Srilata grabbed the offer with both hands and sought leave later to go and fetch her 10th and Intermediate certificates from the Nagarjuna Degree College in Gajwel where she was studying BA and had dropped out way back in 2009. When she reached her college in Gajwel and asked for her certificates, the principal, kind-hearted that he was, pointed out to her that she had just one subject to clear and if she did that, she would have a degree in hand. Again, luck played a dominant role, when the principal informed Srilata that the day happened to be the last date for students to pay examination fee and that he wouldn’t mind extending the time by an hour for Srilata if she was willing to go for it!

Srilata paid the fee, took a little time off work to study, wrote the examination and came out in flying colours, fulfilling the requirement of a minimum of 50 per cent set by Manjulaa Kalyaan. “I never thought that I would see such a major transformation in my life in just a matter of few months. I see Manjulaa Madam virtually as a God who came into my life and changed it forever. I am also grateful to the staff in Swayamkrushi who encouraged and motivated me throughout my struggle,” says a grateful Srilata, who at the time of writing this success story in 2026, was waiting for her B.Ed results.

Srilata, who is confident of getting the B.Ed degree soon, looks forward to teaching the children with intellectual disabilities at the Swayamkrushi school. “I will forever be indebted to Manjulaa Madam not only for the encouragement and motivation but also for bearing the cost of my B.Ed course, continuing to pay my salary and finally, offering me the special educators’ job in the school,” says the young woman, whose supportive mother-in-law also works as an ayah in the organization.

All’s well that ends well, one might say, of Srilata’s journey thus far, but she may just not stop at that. The bubbly and amiable woman, who also worked briefly at McDonald’s, has set her sights on donning the black robe of a lawyer! And she might one day, who knows!

title: NIOS — Boon for Persons with Intellectual Disabilities
filename: NIOS – Boon for Persons with Intellectual Disabilities.docx
excerpt: Arushee is a 27-year-old girl who does three-digit multiplication, is conversant in English and Hindi, and has even walked the ramp! So, what’s the big deal? Well, she happens to be a person with intellectual disabilities, albeit mild. Arus...
paragraphs: Right shoulder

Arushee is a 27-year-old girl who does three-digit multiplication, is conversant in English and Hindi, and has even walked the ramp! So, what’s the big deal? Well, she happens to be a person with intellectual disabilities, albeit mild. Arushee, daughter of an IAF officer, was initially seen as a loner who shunned company, but she now comes across as a very friendly and very helpful person. She even won a gold medal recently for portraying Indira Gandhi at “Taare Zameen Par,” an event organized for persons with disabilities in Hyderabad in August, 2026.

And then you have Thayamma and Sathwik Sai, both persons with intellectual disabilities who took the third spot at “Quizabled,” a competition organized by well-known Bengaluru-based NGO Seva-in-Action for persons with disabilities involving 250 schools from across the five southern States. Thayamma and Sathwik used placards to ‘speak’ on the “Telangana Movement” while participating in the online competition. What makes their win all the more creditable and a major achievement is the fact that first two spots were taken by persons with hearing impairment which meant that their mental faculties were fully functional while both Thayamma and Sathwik are persons with intellectual disabilities. The two also got certificates of merit for scoring 20 out of 20 in the general knowledge section.

Arushee, Thayamma and Sathwik are all students of the National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS) at Swayamkrushi. The organization has two NIOS classes for the nine students with mild intellectual disabilities, but even among them, their capabilities are at different levels. Each student has to be dealt with individually and their study schedule drawn accordingly, say J Parimala Suhasini and Kotaprolu Jayasri, the two NIOS teachers.
There are several other persons with mild intellectual disabilities who have not only brought laurels to the organization but also to the Telangana and nation as a whole.

Suhasini, who joined the organization as a special educator immediately after completing her B.Ed in Special Education, believes that one should have the right aptitude to deal with special children and persons. “I have been involved in social work in rural areas and slums right from my teenage years and the exposure to children with different disabilities virtually decided my future course of action,” says Suhasini, who believes that a friendly disposition, ability to identify areas of interest of students and capability to establish connection with them are essential qualities for a special educator. ‘The ultimate aim is to ensure that whatever I teach them helps them in their lives,” says the multi-talented teacher, who is also a professional singer.

Jayasri, on the other hand, herself has an Autistic daughter, Harika, and in the course of her desperate search for the best-suited place for her daughter, Jayasri, who holds a B.Ed degree, landed in Swayamkrushi. The ever-helpful Manjulaa Kalyaan seeing her situation offered Jayasri a job as teacher and admission for Harika. “It was virtually a case of two birds with one stone for me. It was a blessing since Harika was bullied in the three other special schools she went to earlier, and I had to pull her out. I was desperate and in a state of depression when Swayamkrushi happened in 2024, and it has been smooth sailing since then for both mother and daughter,” says the NIOS teacher with her infectious smile.
Such has been the influence of Manjulaa Kalyaan, Swayamkrushi and the special children on the two NIOS teachers that they feel the organization has become an essential part of their lives!

title: Recipe for Success

paragraphs: (Long form stories)
Recipe for success!

An insatiable hunger to succeed, steely grit to overcome all odds and fire in the belly to fuel ambition - Vishnu Kondoj has all these elements in ample measure and that lifted him from very humble beginnings to steady heights in both career and passion. It may not be the typical, cliched rags-to-riches story, but his journey thus far in 40 years makes a perfect script for what one can achieve if one is focused and hard-working. Vishnu is also quick to acknowledge that had it not been for Manjulaa Kalyaan who played the pivotal role of mentor-motivator in his life, the outcome would have been entirely different.

Son of a carpenter who was associated with Swayamkrushi, Vishnu’s dream was to be successful in life, whatever path it took, and this was evident from his efforts even as a teenager when he supplied milk in his neighbourhood and lent a helping hand to his father, Kumar, in his work. At the core of Vishnu’s heart was art and his passion for it kept popping up at regular intervals.

It was when Vishnu was helping his father in Swayamkrushi that Manjulaa Kalyaan came across the youngster and immediately spotted the talent and zeal in him. The Swayamkrushi founder, who incidentally is perpetually on the lookout for potential talent particularly from the underprivileged sections of society, took Vishnu under her wings to lay the foundation that would transform his life. Like Vishnu’s, there are any number of ‘success stories’ attributed to Manjulaa Kalyaan’s constant efforts to make a difference in people’s lives.

In 2004, Vishnu joined the organization as a vocational trainer and simultaneously did a two-year course in caregivers at the Institute. He was soon promoted as a teacher in special education and won the best teacher award in 2009. Even as he went about his job as a teacher, he also got involved in painting, screen printing and paper bag making units in the organization.
But he had set his sights much higher and went through intermediate, a four-year animation course and a Bachelor’s degree in Fine Arts from JNTU, slogging out at the academics in the evenings.

The next big transformation in his life came in 2009 when he landed a job in Tech Mahindra as a graphic designer. This proved to be the proverbial turning point for Vishnu as the IT major, quick to spot his talent, sent him to Italy on a couple of occasions to further hone his designing skills. The company, impressed by his passion for art and craft, also gave him the opportunity to hold a workshop-cum-exhibition in the company premises. The cherry on the cake was that Mahindra Group chairperson Anand Mahindra was himself present on the occasion!
Vishnu has also held several exhibitions in Delhi, Bengaluru and Hyderabad in the past few years even as he rose to the rank of graphic designer’s team lead in Tech Mahindra.

Vishnu, exposed as he was to persons with intellectual disabilities at Swayamkrushi, always yearned to tap the artistic talent inherent in many persons with disabilities. In 2023, he established the Masterbrush Art Foundation to support the creative talent among the less fortunate people with disabilities. He put together a fabulous management team that has only people with disabilities, be it autism, hearing impaired, Down Syndrome or intellectual disabilities. On July 27 this year, on the occasion of Majulaa Kalyaan’s 85th birthday celebrations, Vishnu launched the Masterbrush Art Foundation website, an initiative that would exclusively further the cause of artists from the disabled community. The website is the only one of its kind in the country and that speaks volumes about Vishnu’s commitment to the cause.

Vishnu’s ultimate goal is to establish a studio-cum-workshop that would serve as an employment platform for the disabled to display and sell their art and craft. He also has plans to launch a Youtube channel in collaboration with Swayamkrushi to bring about awareness on the abundant talent among disabled persons and spread the message on the need for societal inclusiveness.
“Whatever I achieved in life would not have been possible but for the care, attention and motivation I got from Manjulaa Madam,” reiterates the 41-year-old artist in gratitude.

title: A Game of Building Blocks
excerpt: At 50, when most people are chalking out plans for retirement and a relaxed life, Manjulaa Kalyaan had other dreams, big and challenging ones at that, like setting up a school-cum-hostel for persons with intellectual disabilities, particula...
paragraphs: Main body (middle)

At 50, when most people are chalking out plans for retirement and a relaxed life, Manjulaa Kalyaan had other dreams, big and challenging ones at that, like setting up a school-cum-hostel for persons with intellectual disabilities, particularly young adult girls. All she had was tons of qualifications and experience in the field, an innovative and overactive mind, a loving and supportive husband, oodles of true grit, and fierce persuasiveness against which even the most stubborn and strong-willed wilted, a quality that was to come in very handy for her later. Manjulaa Kalyaan also knew that she was playing the game of building blocks that required patience and persistence in ample measure, and she made sure she nurtured these qualities.

Swayamkrushi, her dream NGO project, was born in a four-bedroom house in Ishaque Colony in 1991, and had just two girls with intellectual disabilities to start with. She decided to take in four boys with intellectual disabilities as day scholars in the schools. She took in a girl, a fresh graduate, and trained and taught her the finer points of teaching children with intellectual difficulties. She also brought in two care-givers from the Thakur Hari Prasad Institute, another NGO in the city. Then began her journey of shifting houses as the strength of both students as well as resident girls increased. In a way, she had already initiated the concept of Group Home long before it was recognized under the Inclusive Act in 2007.

Cut to 2026, Swayamkrushi which Manjulaa Kalyaan had dared to dream in 1991, is now a full-blown Not-for-Profit Organisation which is home to about 75 persons, mostly young adult girls with intellectual disabilities and a school with a total strength of about 150. The organization, now located in its own five-acre campus in Jawahar Nagar, also conducts a two-year B.Ed in Special Education (Intellectual Disabilities) and boasts of a staff strength of about 70.

It was a tough journey, but Manjulaa Kalyaan, now 85, is still a sprightly lady chasing her dream, tracking down donors, chalking out plans for expansion, training teachers, personally inspecting classrooms and kitchen and the likes. Ask her about a turning point and she will say that there are more than one. “In my initial days of struggle, Puli Balaram, a BJP leader who was a member of the Punjagutta Sai Baba temple committee, came to my help pledging to take care of one teacher’s salary besides donating a television set. Then around 94/95, I managed to get Central government grant to run the school, and the strength started growing since I also had to establish physiotherapy and speech therapy units with the strength growing to about 35 then. Around this time, I was also made a member of the National Trust,” recalls the octogenarian founder-director of Swayamkrushi.

Her husband, Wing Commander Kalyan Sundaram, who had taken voluntary retirement from the IAF, was also a huge source of support and motivation for her. “I used his entire pension to run the school in those days. In fact, the staff used to jokingly refer to him as ‘donation unlimited.’ Along the way, Jairam Reddy, a philanthropist, also helped a lot by way of allowing us to run the hostel-cum-school in his flats in Trimulgherry,” Manjulaa Kalyaan says.

Today, both the hostel and school are run very professionally. The class strength has been restricted to a mere five against the government guideline of eight, to ensure individual attention to each student. The school also has nine students presently in two classes under the National Institute of Open Schooling (NIOS). Even in the hostel, every room has an attached washroom, and has just two adult girls with one care-giver. “I was against the concept of dormitory from the beginning and wanted these girls to have their own private space, particularly given their condition,” says Manjulaa Kalyaan.

Swayamkrushi also has a unique ‘Parent Homes’ under which parents of children with intellectual disabilities can take on lease one-bedroom units built within the campus. These children attend classes and other activities in the schools during the day and return to their parents in the evening. “The unique feature of this facility is that the parents can continue to stay in the unit for their lifetime if the child passes away, and in the event of the parents passing away, we take care of the child for life,” points out Manjulaa Kalyaan.
It was these efforts of Manjulaa Kalyaan that the Central government recognized and appreciated and bestowed her with not one but four national awards in different years.

title: Art — The Great Equaliser
excerpt: Art, they say, is the great equalizer. Nothing describes better the creative expressions of Bharati Saini, a 25-year-old bubbly girl, an artist from Uttarakhand, who draws and paints using just her elbow stumps. Fate changed the path for Bh...
paragraphs: For Right Shoulder

Art, they say, is the great equalizer. Nothing describes better the creative expressions of Bharati Saini, a 25-year-old bubbly girl, an artist from Uttarakhand, who draws and paints using just her elbow stumps. Fate changed the path for Bharati when she, as a playful 11-year-old girl, picked up an object that turned out to be an explosive device apparently meant to scare away animals. The consequent blast ripped through her upper limbs, leaving her with just elbow stumps after amputation.

Completely undeterred by the loss of her limbs in the ‘accident,’ Bharathi, then a sixth standard student, returned to school in just a month-and-half with her elbow stumps still bandaged. Subsequently, she found her voice in art, and her drawings and paintings using just her elbow stumps were soon the talk of the town. The proverbial turning point for Bharati came when she was in 10th standard. The District Magistrate who was visiting the school was impressed by her paintings and casually suggested that she pursue her interest seriously by taking up fine art in graduation. Bharati, who was then not even aware about the existence of such a degree, joined Nainital University for her Bachelor’s degree in Fine Art and later Master’s from Kurukshetra University in Haryana.

Bharati’s journey in art brought her to Hyderabad recently, and she is currently teaching drawing and painting to persons with intellectual disabilities at Swayamkrushi. “Working with these people gives me immense satisfaction, and it appears to be a two-way street. My students are very reluctant to leave my art class when it is time for them to go to other classes,” says a beaming Bharati, who came to Hyderabad to help friend and fellow artist Vishnu Kondoj set up a studio-cum-workshop under the aegis of Masterbrush Art Foundation. She is a member of the core team of Masterbrush and has participated in several art exhibitions across the country.

Bharati has a total of about 25 students who are at different levels of intellectual disabilities. She restricts each class to about five students since it is easier to handle them then. She usually has five batches of students attending her art class every day and she helps them with basic drawing and colouring, often leaving them to use their own imagination and inherent creativity.

“A lot of people have helped me reach the position I am in now, and I would like to give back to society, and what better way than work with persons with intellectual disabilities at Swayamkrushi. Initially, I was a bit skeptical but the organisation’s founder-director Manjulaa Kalyaan and all the other wonderful staff here put me at ease, and I am enjoying staying and working here,” says Bharati, who basically speaks only Hindi.

Isn’t language a barrier for her? “Not at all. I explain to my students using signs and in case of any difficulty, I take the help of one of the teachers to explain in Telugu,” says Bharti, who goes on to point out that the students, despite their disabilities, even insist on putting up some of the drawings on the wall fully realizing that it would be a difficult task for her. “Their level of understanding is fascinating for me,” she adds.

Incidentally, her handicap notwithstanding, Bharati also excels in mehendi and tailoring. “In fact, I was applying mehendi to all the girls and teachers on the eve of Raksha Bandhan. I applied mehendi even for Manjulaa Madam,” she says with a smile.
So, what are her plans for the future? “I don’t know what the future holds for me. But I am very happy working and staying in Swayamkrushi for now," Bharati asserts.

title: Chance Encounter That Changed My Life
excerpt: A chance encounter with Dr Maria Egg-Benes, a renowned special educator from Switzerland, at a workshop in Bengaluru, turned out to be the turning point in my life, and a defining moment which revealed the path I was to take to serve the le...
paragraphs: Direct Speak

A chance encounter with Dr Maria Egg-Benes, a renowned special educator from Switzerland, at a workshop in Bengaluru, turned out to be the turning point in my life, and a defining moment which revealed the path I was to take to serve the less fortunate ones in society. That was in 1969, and being married to an Air Force officer took me to various cities including New Delhi, Chennai and Hyderabad. My transition from a teacher in a regular school teaching normal children to that of a special educator caring for the intellectually challenged took shape in New Delhi where I joined Amrit Kaur Bal Vihar, popularly known as Okhla Centre. The seven years that I spent at the Centre laid a strong foundation and prepared me for the tough journey that I would be facing in the years ahead.

Later, we moved to Hyderabad and subsequently Chennai, and in both the cities, I was involved with the Durgabhai Deshmukh Vocational Training Centre. While working in Hyderabad, I converted the Centre which essentially imparted training to women with physical disabilities into an integrated agency to include women with intellectual disabilities. In 1984, my husband and I decided to make Hyderabad our home and that is when my early calling took wings. After obtaining a Master’s in Special Education from the University of Pittsburgh in the US, I returned to India with a strong desire to make a difference in the lives of the intellectually-challenged persons in the county, further their cause and bring about awareness among the people. There was no dearth of career opportunities in the US but my country was a priority for me.

With close to two decades of quality service in the field and armed with sufficient academic qualifications, my next stop was the National Institute for the Mentally Handicapped in Secunderabad as a lecturer, where I conceived a ‘Post School Programme’ for women over the age of 18 with developmental challenges. Under the programme, these women were trained in activities of daily living that included home maintenance besides equipping them with skills to make them work-ready. The programme was an instant success but restricted as I was by the Institute’s broader functions, I decided to break-free and go on my own path.

Thus was born Swayamkrushi in 1989 that finally allowed me to realise my dream of not only fostering independent and dignified living of the intellectually-challenged but also integrate them with the community in general and society at large. In the course of the four decades of its existence till now, Swayamkrushi has grown into a much sought after organisation running a school for the intellectually disabled, a hostel for women and offering B. Ed course in Special Education that is affiliated to Osmania University, among several other activities. Simultaneously, I also launched initiatives to increase awareness and bring about sensitivity towards those with intellectual disabilities.
Direct Speak
Group Homes – Pioneering initiative that catapulted Swayamkrushi into higher orbit

In a pioneering initiative in the country, I conceived the idea of group homes which would house eight women (all above the age of 18) with different levels of intellectual disabilities, living together akin to extended Indian families. Each single group comprises three women in the mild range, four in moderate range and one from the severe range. The first seven are trained to take care of the house as also the woman with severe challenges. And I am proud to say that Swayamkrushi had established eight such homes, all located in residential colonies that are in close proximity to the Institute to facilitate their participation in the institute’s training sessions and classes. The number, however, has now dropped to five on account of rising rent and other cost factors.

When I started setting up the Group Homes, there was quite a bit of resistance from the people in the colonies who were not comfortable about women with intellectual disabilities living amongst them. I had to put in a lot of effort to convince them that inclusiveness was essential in society and that people with various forms of disabilities had to be accommodated and included in the social mainstream. Over time, the residents accepted the women and even helped them when the need arose.

Particularly satisfying for me is the fact that following the success of the Group Homes concept and the training programmes, I had advocated and pioneered inclusion of the intellectually challenged way back in 1991, a full 16 years before the Inclusion Act was ratified by the Government of India and the United Nations in 2007.

Along the way, I authored two textbooks for B. Ed course, co-authored four UNICEF-funded manuals for Learning Disabilities, received a Doctorate in Special Education from Indian Virtual University in 2019, presented numerous papers on various related topics and received awards from President APJ Abdul Kalam and Vice President M Venkaiah Naidu.
With 55 years of service in Special Education behind me, I continue to be as active and involved in the field even now at 85 as I was when I set out to achieve my goals.
(Direct Speak - Manjulaa Kalyaan’s blog)
Women’s empowerment - A byproduct of Swayamkrushi

I have always felt that women’s empowerment, particularly those from the impoverished sections and lower strata of society, was an essential part of the development process. If one were to study the staff profile in Swayamkrushi, they would realise that 95 per cent of the staff are women, most of them from the economically weaker section of society. Initially, most of the women working in the organisation were destitutes with no one to care for them or no place to call home.

When the new campus at Jawahar Nagar started coming up, most of the people (read women) I employed were from neighbouring areas. I personally took upon the task of training them for specific jobs based on their background, aptitude and skill levels. They are placed in various roles such as care-givers, ayahs, cooks and gardeners.

Many of them have been with the organisation right from inception and form the backbone of the Swayamkrushi family. A special feature of the work ethics in the organisation is total recognition of dignity of labour. Everyone does whatever is required without complaining, irrespective of whether it is part of their job profile. You may find a teacher or the speech therapist helping in moving furniture, taking an unwell girl to the hospital or even slipping into the role of a driver.

I make it a point to identify and select at least two women from the existing staff every year and train them for higher and better paying roles. Take for example the case of Srilatha. She joined the organisation as a sweeper after completing her intermediate. I realised the girl had potential and put her through the B.Ed course in the Institute free of cost. Today, she is a special educator handling children with intellectual disabilities. Similarly, Aruna was working as a gardener but I made her go through the B.Ed course and like Srilatha, she too is a teacher in the organisation now.
There are several such cases in Swayamkrushi, and some have even found very good jobs outside. That for me is real empowerment of women, and it gives me immense satisfaction!

title: Dairy for a Purpose!
excerpt: If you are a resident of Swayamkrushi or a guest staying in the campus overnight, you will most likely wake up to the mooing by the small herd of cows, a little distance away from the main building in the campus. Ksheerabdi, Laxmi and Ganga...
paragraphs: Fun Facts – Left Shoulder

If you are a resident of Swayamkrushi or a guest staying in the campus overnight, you will most likely wake up to the mooing by the small herd of cows, a little distance away from the main building in the campus. Ksheerabdi, Laxmi and Ganga are ready to begin the day, waiting for Prabhakar Reddy from the neighbouring village to come and milk them. He is usually in by 5 AM and is ready with two pails containing about six litres of fresh milk which he delivers to the kitchen by 6.30 AM.

“We started the dairy in a small way in 2022 when one Mr Reddy donated two cows. That set the trend and many people came forward to donate cows. We now have a total of six cows and three calves,” says Manjulaa Kalyaan, the founder-director of Swayamkrushi.

The octogenarian founder goes on to point out that the idea is to be self-sufficient in all aspects and dairy is an important component in that direction. “We lost one cow, but then the owner of Gandhian School in Trimulgherry, who had a small dairy farm, donated four cows. We now have enough cows for our needs but I want to expand the dairy farm and make it a revenue generating unit since the organization is constantly in need of funds for its daily functioning,” says Manjulaa, adding that at present, the cows are housed in a shed close to the gate. The plan is to shift them further inside the campus once the new building comes up adjacent to the existing block.

Manjulaa Kalyaan is keen that the residents in the hostel - women with intellectual disabilities – eventually learn to take care of the cows. Incidentally, Ksheerabdi means ‘milk aplenty’ and it was Manjulaa Kalyaan who came up with this name for one of the cows.

title: Destination Kadiam, for Plants
excerpt: Whenever Manjulaa Kalyaan plans to do something for Swayamkrushi, she ensures that it is the best in the market, so much so that when she wanted to add a little greenery to the newly-acquired five-acre campus in Jawahar Nagar, she drove all...
paragraphs: (Fun Facts)

Whenever Manjulaa Kalyaan plans to do something for Swayamkrushi, she ensures that it is the best in the market, so much so that when she wanted to add a little greenery to the newly-acquired five-acre campus in Jawahar Nagar, she drove all the way to Kadiam in Andhra Pradesh to fetch the choicest of saplings. Not many may know that Kadiam is well known all over the country for its numerous nurseries selling the best varieties of fruit-bearing, flowering, ornamental and even some rare plants.

That was in 2016, when the organization decided to construct its own building in the vast new campus. “I wanted to plant all the saplings before the building came up to ensure fully-grown trees all around when the place finally becomes operational. My US-based sister, who was visiting me at that time, wanted to fund the greening operation, and we decided to go to Kadiam which has the country’s biggest and best nurseries to get the saplings” recalls Manjulaa Kalyaan.

The sisters, who picked up Jayalakshmi en route for her knowledge of AP, completed the saplings shopping spree in just one day, covering over 800 kms. They bought various varieties of mangoes, chikus (sapota), pomegranate, sweet lemon, amla, water apple, among other fruit-bearing trees. They also bought several other plants including Maredu (Bilva) which is considered special for Lord Shiva.

They have all grown into huge trees and form a beautiful mini-forest right in front of the main building door. They not only bear delicious fruits but also provide ample shade that has become the ideal spot for many of the staff to spend leisure time or to have lunch. “All the produce including the King of Fruits (mangoes) are strictly meant for in-house consumption, and the children enjoy the fruit season. We also make our own pickles,” says Manjulaa Kalyaan.

“We also got teak and bamboo saplings from the forest department that we planted along the boundary wall,” says Manjulaa Kalyaan, who goes on to add that she may have to make a trip to Kadiam soon to get more plants before the construction of the organisation’s second building is taken up.

Manjulaa Kalyaan also points out that till recently, they were also growing vegetables including brinjal, tomatoes, okra and several leafy varieties. “We had to abandon vegetable cultivation when a small hillock in the campus was demolished, and that threw up unimaginable quantities of rock,” she says.

The garden and the trees are taken care of by T Naveen, a 27-year-old youngster from Mahabubnagar who joined the organization as a watchman in 2023. Today, he is a jack-of-all-trades kind of guy who is willing to lend a helping hand wherever it’s needed.

title: Exercise of a Different Kind
excerpt: “Their unqualified innocence and unconditional love for me conquered my heart,” says J Priyadarshini, the physiotherapist at Swayamkrushi, of the special children she has been treating, putting them through a set of daily exercises. The gen...
paragraphs: Right Shoulder

“Their unqualified innocence and unconditional love for me conquered my heart,” says J Priyadarshini, the physiotherapist at Swayamkrushi, of the special children she has been treating, putting them through a set of daily exercises. The genial 32-year-old holds a Bachelor’s Degree in Physiotherapy that she acquired after four-and-half years of academics and internships, something that is as taxing and grinding as a medical course.

Priyadarshini’s face lights up when she talks about her job that is a clear reflection of her love for the profession and particularly being with the special children who are under her wings at the physiotherapy unit in Swayamkrushi. “Most of the children who come to me are afflicted with cerebral palsy, autism and down syndrome and some with intellectual disabilities. I take them in batches of 10, one kid per 45-minute session per day and the treatment may go on for a month or two or even longer, depending on the severity of the child’s condition,” explains Priyadarshini, who joined the organization in 2023.

The physiotherapy unit is well equipped with treadmill, static cycle, shoulder pulleys, finger ladder and other smaller instruments that are used to help the children with their exercises. The physiotherapist, who has helped dozens of children ‘loosen up’ in the past three years, says their initial hesitation and apprehension disappear when they start using the various equipment. “In fact, there are some children who enter the unit and start doing their exercises even without my saying anything or helping them which clearly indicates their level of understanding. The exercises are basically aimed at muscle strengthening, increasing flexibility, posture correction and helping mobility,” says Priyadarshini.

Priyadarshini does not care to hide her emotions when she speaks of the time when she was working in various hospitals before she landed in Swayamkrushi. “I feel I belong here, and I tremendously enjoy the time I spend with these children. In my earlier jobs, people I treated were just patients with problems but here in Swayamkrushi, it’s very different since I deal with special children that invariably ends in developing an attachment for them. I must confess though that I did have a sense of trepidation when I first came in but it soon vanished once I started interacting with the children, and there has been no looking back since then,” she says with a broad smile.

But, how does she manage with the children given their condition? “Yes, at times it is difficult but that is precisely the sort of challenge that I enjoy. I am stern when I need to be and pamper them when they do what they are required to without a fuss. The children feel comfortable after coming for a few days,” says the physiotherapist.

And the success rate? “Well, take the case of Shanvi, a 12-year-old girl with cerebral palsy. All four of her limbs had no strength but now after weeks of constant physiotherapy, she is able to walk a bit with a little help and a walker. Similarly, Umaimah, again a 12-year-old girl, could not stand up when she came to me. There was just no strength in her lower limbs and she would fall down when she attempted to stand. But after months of exercise, she is now able to walk like any other girl her age and that too without the help of a walker,” says a beaming Priyadarshini, adding that Umaimah’s parents were thrilled at the drastic improvement.

“For me, the reward in my profession is when I see even a little improvement in a special child from a near hopeless situation. It really is amazing to see the transformation in some children after constant physiotherapy, and that keeps me going,” says the physiotherapist, who like most others in the organization, feels completely at home in Swayamkrushi.

title: Kitchen — Beehive of Activity
excerpt: The kitchen in Swayamkrushi is a beehive of activity right from 5 AM in the morning when the cooks and other kitchen staff start arriving. By 5.30 AM, the stoves are lit and fresh, aromatic tea is served to everyone around. The staff, compr...
paragraphs: (Right Shoulder)

The kitchen in Swayamkrushi is a beehive of activity right from 5 AM in the morning when the cooks and other kitchen staff start arriving. By 5.30 AM, the stoves are lit and fresh, aromatic tea is served to everyone around. The staff, comprising two cooks and three assistants, begin preparation for breakfast for 80-odd persons by 7 AM. Breakfast is typically a south Indian fare – idly, dosa, upma, pongal etc with accompaniments.

“I come in by 5 AM to ensure that breakfast and milk is ready for the residents who start trooping in along with their care-givers by 7 AM. Once breakfast is done with, we immediately start preparations for lunch, which is usually for around 150 persons including the day scholars in schools,” says I Sharada, the person in-charge of the spacious kitchen section. The dining tables and chairs are made of steel and each table can seat six persons. What is impressive is that both the dining hall and the kitchen area are kept clean, with the ayahs and helpers constantly cleaning the place. Dinner is cooked early and kept ready for the 80-odd residents before the cooks leave for the day at around 5 PM.

The lunch is simple but nutritious comprising either sambar or dal, a vegetable side dish, white rice and yoghurt. On festival says and special occasions of course, everyone is treated to special lunch that will typically include a sweet too. “On an average, we cook about 17 kg of rice and use about 10 kg of vegetables for the dishes every day. Besides, there is similar quantity of lentils consumed every day,” says Sarada, who joined Swayamkrushi in 2018 as assistant cook.

Sarada says since enjoys her work and feels very happy when some of the children come to her and appreciate a particular dish. “Nothing is more rewarding for a cook than someone appreciating the dishes, and more so if it comes from a person with intellectual disabilities,” says the head cook.
